checks.claim: Key: with the middle hole moved out of line, the spot disappears from the wall (light cannot bend round the card)
checks.note: SERC (grades 3-6): lined-up holes let the light through; 'If the middle card is moved to one side so that the holes are not lined up the light cannot bend around the middle card.'

checks.claim: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium (context)
checks.note: 'light rays travel in straight lines ... through a uniform, isotropic medium.' Diffraction at a hole's edge is negligible at this scale; the context's 'cannot bend around the card' is the standard and true classroom claim.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It stays just where it was' / 'It slides over with the card' / 'It grows dimmer but stays put'
checks.note: The stem says the hole is moved out of line (not part way), so no straight path through all three holes remains; no spot stays, slides or dims. The first and third cards' holes do not move, so the spot cannot follow the middle card.

checks.claim: Key: an object is seen when light reflected from it enters the eyes
checks.note: NGSS PS4.B: 'An object can be seen when light reflected from its surface enters the eyes.' England Year 6 agrees: objects are seen because they give out or reflect light into the eye.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Light goes out from his eyes to the chair' (emission theory); context 'Eyes send out no light'
checks.note: Emission (extramission) theory of Euclid and Ptolemy, rejected by Ibn al-Haytham; vision is passive reception of light entering the eye. (Cats' eyeshine is reflection, not emission.)

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The chair gives off a faint light of its own'
checks.note: A room-temperature object's thermal radiation is essentially all infrared, which is invisible and is not what lets him see the chair; visible glow needs hundreds of degrees C. Wrong at the grade's meaning of 'light'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Light passes through the chair to his eyes'
checks.note: Virginia grade 5: 'Examples of opaque materials include metal, wood, bricks'.

checks.claim: Context: in a room with no light at all he would see nothing
checks.note: England Year 3: 'they need light in order to see things and that dark is the absence of light'.

checks.claim: Key: paper bounces light off in every direction (diffuse reflection), so it shows no clear picture
checks.note: 'scattering of light rays in multiple directions upon encountering a rough or irregular surface'; paper is named for its fibrous texture; diffuse reflection forms no sharp image. 'Every direction' is a fair 5th-grade rendering of 'many directions'.

checks.claim: Context: mirror is smooth and reflects in an orderly way, making a clear picture
checks.note: Specular reflection on a smooth surface 'enabling clear image formation'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It does not reflect any light at all'
checks.note: White objects diffusely reflect all visible wavelengths nearly equally; Kesler TEKS 5.8C: 'Almost everything reflects some light.'

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It lets all the light pass straight through' / 'It needs much brighter light to show one'
checks.note: Paper lets a little light through but reflects most; brightness does not turn diffuse reflection into an image.

checks.claim: Context: scattered light is how people see paper and most other things
checks.note: 'enables the visibility of color, texture, and shape for most everyday objects'.

checks.claim: Key: the straw looks broken because light bends as it goes from water into air (refraction)
checks.note: A partly submerged straw or pencil 'appears bent at the water's surface' because light from the underwater part bends on entering air; Kesler TEKS 5.8C says the same. (Strictly the light also crosses the glass wall; the simplification stays true.)

checks.claim: Context: light travels more slowly in water than in air
checks.note: Refractive index of water about 1.33, air about 1.

checks.claim: Wrong: water's weight bends the straw / light bounces back off the top of the water / water soaks up the light
checks.note: The straw is straight; the broken look is refraction, not reflection or absorption. (The underside of the water surface can reflect when seen from below, but that does not make the straw look broken from the side.)

checks.claim: Key: the bending of light as it passes through the lens is called refraction
checks.note: A magnifying glass is a convex lens that works by refraction and forms an enlarged virtual image.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Magnification' (is it partly right as the name for the bending?)
checks.note: Magnification is 'the process by which the apparent size of an object is increased through optical means', which curved mirrors can do as well as lenses; it is the result (the ant looking bigger), not the name of the bending. The stem asks for 'this bending of light', so magnification is wrong. It is the strongest distractor, which is fair.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Reflection' / 'Absorption'
checks.note: Light passes through the lens and bends; it is not bounced back or soaked up.

checks.claim: Stem: 'A magnifying glass is a lens made of clear, curved glass'
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a bi-convex lens made from glass or high-index plastic', acrylic also used. 'Made of glass' is the classic case, not an error; optional tweak 'usually made of clear, curved glass'.

checks.claim: Context: refraction is light bending as it passes from one material into another, e.g. air into glass
Key: a prism spreading sunlight into a band of colours shows sunlight is a mix of many colours
checks.note: Newton: white light is 'a heterogeneous mixture of distinct colored rays'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It has no colours until the glass adds them'
checks.note: Hooke's modification theory; refuted when a second prism recombined the colours into white.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It is pale yellow light'
checks.note: Sunlight 'appears white to the human eye when integrated across its spectrum'; NASA (https://eclipse2017.nasa.gov/what-color-sun): white seen from above the atmosphere, yellowish only through the air. In any case a prism's band of colours does not show yellowness.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It is a mix of just red, yellow and blue'
checks.note: Sunlight disperses into 'a continuous spectrum of colors ranging from red to violet'; RYB are painters' primaries, RGB the primaries of light.

checks.claim: Context: sunlight looks white but is a mix of all the colours of the rainbow
checks.note: Virginia grade 5: a prism disperses white light into its colours; 'The sum of these colors is white light.'

checks.claim: Context: prism bends violet most and red least
checks.note: 'Violet rays exhibit the greatest deviation ... red rays bend least.'

checks.claim: Context: a second prism turned the other way gathers the colours back into white light
checks.note: UNSW (J. Wolfe) reproduces Newton's recombination with an inverted second prism; Grokipedia Opticks agrees. One paper (Garcia-Molina et al.) notes it is clean only when the prisms are set close; the context's plain claim stands.

checks.claim: Key: the black shirt warms more because it absorbs more of the sunlight
checks.note: Illinois physics: dark clothes 'absorb most of the light that hits them'; that energy 'is changed into heat'; white clothing 'simply reflects more of the light'. Kesler TEKS 5.8C: black T-shirt absorbs sunlight and turns it into heat; white reflects most and stays cooler.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It pulls in more heat from the air'
checks.note: Truly wrong. Colour (albedo) governs how much sunlight a surface absorbs, not heat taken from the air; heat flow between air and shirt depends on their temperature difference, so the hotter black shirt, if anything, takes LESS heat from the air (it loses heat to it). Fabrics' thermal-infrared emissivity is about 0.88 whatever the fabric (Belliveau et al. 2020, Textile Research Journal), so the black dye does not make it soak up more heat radiation from warm surroundings either. Both girls stand in the same air, as the context says.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It reflects more of the sunlight' / 'It lets more sunlight pass through'
checks.note: Reflecting or transmitting more would leave it cooler, and black absorbs rather than transmits.

checks.claim: Stem: the black shirt grows much warmer in an hour of hot sun
checks.note: Standard result; outdoor shirt tests report dark shirts tens of degrees F hotter than white.

checks.claim: Context: dark things absorb most of the light; absorbed light turns into heat; the white shirt reflects more away
checks.note: 'Most', not 'all', as the fact sheet's caution requires.

checks.claim: Key: the apple looks red because it reflects red light and absorbs the rest
checks.note: 'a pigment appearing red absorbs shorter wavelengths like blue and green' and reflects the red. Grokipedia Color: colour 'results from the selective reflection, absorption, or emission of light'. 'Absorbs the rest' is the standard grade-5 phrasing; the context hedges to 'most of the other colours'. Optional tightening: 'absorbs most of the rest'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It absorbs red light and reflects the rest'
checks.note: Reversed; such a surface would look blue-green (cyan), not red.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It gives off red light of its own'
checks.note: An apple is not a light source; its colour is reflected sunlight. (Any chlorophyll fluorescence in apple skin is tiny, is driven by absorbed light, and is not why it looks red; not defensible at this level.)

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It turns all of the white light into red light'
checks.note: The other colours are absorbed, not converted to red.

checks.claim: Stem: white sunlight holds light of every colour
checks.note: 'white light is a composite of these separable components' (Newton).

checks.claim: Context: a white thing reflects nearly all the colours, a black thing absorbs nearly all of them
checks.note: White objects reflect all visible wavelengths nearly equally; 'nearly' keeps the black claim safe.

checks.claim: Key: the shadow is star-shaped because light travels in straight lines
checks.note: England Year 6: 'use the idea that light travels in straight lines to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Light bends around the star's edges'
checks.note: Light does diffract very slightly at edges, but that would blur the outline, not make it; as the reason for the same shape it is wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The star reflects its shape onto the wall' / 'The star's darkness spreads onto the wall'
checks.note: A shadow is 'a dark area on a surface where light from a light source is blocked by an object', a silhouette; the star's lit face points at the lamp, not the wall.

checks.claim: Context: the star blocks the light that hits it; light just missing its edges goes straight on, so the dark patch has the star's outline; a shadow is a place the light cannot reach
checks.note: Matches the definition and silhouette; the context does not claim sharp edges, so it survives the wide-source blur caution.

unit_notes: All nine questions pass. Four focus points checked: (1) red apple: every wrong choice is wrong; the key's 'absorbs the rest' is standard grade-5 phrasing, optional tightening to 'absorbs most of the rest' to match the context and the unit's no-absolutes caution. (2) Black shirt: 'pulls in more heat from the air' is truly wrong (colour sets sunlight absorbed; heat from air depends on temperature difference, and fabric IR emissivity is about 0.88 regardless). (3) Magnifying glass: 'Magnification' is the result (apparent size enlarged, also done by mirrors), not the name of the bending, so it is wrong for 'this bending of light'; stem's 'made of clear, curved glass' is the classic case (many are plastic), optional 'usually'. (4) Prism and white light: Newton's dispersion and inverted-prism recombination confirmed; sunlight looks white (Grokipedia Sunlight, NASA).
